## Counting money against counting people
Two different figures circulate for the same quarter.

TransUnion put credit card delinquency of 90 days or more at 2.5% for the first quarter of 2026, close to three times below the New York Fed figure.
Both are correct. They count different things.
The New York Fed measures overdue balances as a share of all card balances. TransUnion measures overdue borrowers as a share of all card borrowers.
People who fall behind tend to owe more, so counting by money produces a much larger share. Without checking which figure is on the table, two people can describe the same quarter in opposite terms.

@@REF@@US consumer credit market increasingly splitting along a K shaped path (TransUnion, 2026-04-30)|https://newsroom.transunion.com/k-shaped-q1-2026-ciir/|https://content.presspage.com/uploads/1104/47fd0a36-c08e-442c-b3af-546dd16c6101/1920_girl-holding-card-hand-paying-450w-2629574219.jpg?10000

## The top and the bottom are pulling apart
What TransUnion points at is not the average but the split.

The super prime tier grew to 40.7% of consumers by the fourth quarter of 2025, up 3.8 percentage points from the fourth quarter of 2019.
At the other end the subprime tier is growing and the middle is thinning out.
A flat headline delinquency rate can be the arithmetic of an improving top offsetting a deteriorating bottom.
One average line hides that motion. Schiff's sentence and any rebuttal that answers it with the average alone share the same blind spot.

Card balances themselves stand at $1.252 trillion, down $25 billion on the quarter and up $70 billion on the year.
The denominator under that percentage keeps growing.

## The August release of the Q2 report decides it
The next print settles this argument.

The New York Fed publishes the same report every quarter, and second quarter data lands within August.
A reading above 7.5% ends five quarters of flatness and hands the direction to Schiff. A reading below 7.5% means the plateau held.
Neither outcome changes the level, which is the highest stretch since 2011. Whether things are getting worse and whether they are already bad are separate questions, and today's data answers the second one.

Most of what those two booked was not money earned by selling anything.

When an asset a company has not sold rises in value, accounting rules require that increase to be recorded as income in that quarter. That is an unrealised gain.
No cash arrives, and the net income line grows anyway.

A painting on your wall getting more valuable does not raise your salary that year. Corporate accounting still writes the increase into the profit line.

meru-skhynix-one-share-hyperliquid-liqui:
At 8:00 on the morning of July 28, one SK hynix share traded at 1,272,000 won. That was nearly 30% below the previous close, the lowest price the stock was allowed to reach that day.

The share filled immediately and the price was back above 1.7 million won soon after. In the Korean market that was the end of it.

Outside Korea it was not. On a market that used the same price as its reference, 960 accounts and $57.4 million were closed out in two minutes.

## Eight in the morning, when the book is thinnest

The Korea Exchange opens its regular session at nine. NextTrade, which opened in 2025 as a second venue where the same shares change hands, runs its own pre-open session from 8:00 to 8:50. The Seoul Economic Daily reported that this single share filled there rather than on the Korea Exchange.

@@REF@@SK hynix single-share limit trade triggers 83 billion won crypto futures liquidation (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-07-30)|https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/07/30/sk-hynix-single-share-limit-trade-triggers-83-billion-won|https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/07/30/news-p.v1.20260730.9a7844d0e68446278f0d4efc939778e7_P1.png

It is the hour when Korean stocks trade at their thinnest. One price printed in a window with almost no buyers and no sellers became the day's reference.

## The price was picked up outside the border

Money is bet on SK hynix outside Korea too, through perpetual futures, contracts with no expiry. Nothing changes hands but the direction of the price, so a market can be opened anywhere, whether or not the stock is listed there.

One of the places these markets open is Hyperliquid. It is not an exchange run by a company with staff; it is a program written in advance that runs itself by fixed rules.

Whoever opens the market is a separate party. The SK hynix market was opened by trade.xyz, and trade.xyz also chose where the price would come from. It chose NextTrade.

## A seat that clears out on a 5% move

One of the rules trade.xyz set was 10x leverage: a million won of your own money carries a ten million won bet. Leverage comes with a maintenance margin line, and when equity falls below it the exchange does not wait, it closes the position on the spot. At 10x that line sits around 5%.

The reference price fell from $1,127.90 to $917.25, a drop of 18.7%.

A 5% line met an 18.7% move. There was only one outcome.

## No one broke a rule

Hyperliquid said it provides the rails and that the party opening a market sets the price rules, BeInCrypto reported. The guard trade.xyz had set allowed a 10% move at once, plus one reset, for a maximum of 19%. The actual move stayed inside that band, so the guard worked as designed.

@@REF@@Hyperliquid explains $57 million SK Hynix perp liquidations after a price feed anomaly (BeInCrypto, 2026-07-28)|https://beincrypto.com/hyperliquid-sk-hynix-perp-oracle-liquidations/|https://assets.beincrypto.com/img/9bSbOmyA4HHmwqtR8v-GH2122BQ=/1200x630/smart/filters:format(jpeg):quality(82)/2dcb42bf99444cbc8e0debfdfd30acc2

Working as designed is not the same as nothing happening. Of the $57.4 million closed out, actual losses are estimated at about $17.3 million, and 100 accounts positioned for a fall on the other side were automatically cut by $10.8 million.

Opening a market requires depositing 500,000 HYPE, about $27.4 million, with Hyperliquid. Validators can vote to burn that deposit. The burned money does not go to the investors who lost. trade.xyz said it would cover the forced-liquidation losses in full and change how it computes the price, but that was its own choice, not something the rules compelled.

## Whether one share is enough next time is decided here

What settles it is where the price comes from. If a single fill from the thin pre-open window still passes through untouched, the same thing happens again. If it changes to a blend of venues or an average over a set period, this was one operator's setting.

Where a stock is listed and how far its price travels are now two different questions.

How far that price travels is something nobody decides any more.

The design data rate of the first LPDDR6 that China's CXMT has built is 12,800 megabits per second.
SK hynix, preparing the same standard, is targeting 14,400, and the limit of the lithography China can get its hands on sits inside that difference.

The same piece adds that SK hynix holds the most advanced publicly disclosed position and is preparing mass production in the second half of this year.

## What LPDDR6 is and why the speed matters

LPDDR is the low-power DRAM soldered directly onto the board of a phone or a laptop, and LPDDR6 is its newest generation.
Unlike the stick that slots into a server, it is fixed inside the device, so it cannot be swapped later and the speed chosen at purchase stays for the life of the machine.

Speed is written as how many megabits move per second.
The more AI work a device runs locally, the more the bottleneck becomes fetching stored values, so this number decides what class of product a chip can go into.

## Why the top of the standard stays out of reach

@@REF@@CXMT nears LPDDR6 production: the DUV ceiling shows up in the 12.8 Gbps vs 14.4 Gbps gap (TechTimes, 2026-08-02)|https://www.techtimes.com/articles/322700/20260802/cxmt-nears-lpddr6-production-duv-ceiling-shows-128-gbps-vs-144-gbps-gap.htm|https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/471043/photo-shows-view-changxin-memory-technologies-factory.jpg

TechTimes traces the gap to how the circuits get printed.
SK hynix prints in a single pass with extreme-ultraviolet tools at a 13.5 nanometer wavelength, while CXMT layers several passes with deep-ultraviolet tools at a longer wavelength.

Layering passes means aligning the plate again each time, and a little misalignment accumulates with every pass.
That accumulated error shaves the top speed the finished circuit can hold.
The ceiling gets cut off during the sorting step, where finished parts are binned by the speed they actually reach.

China has not been able to bring in a single extreme-ultraviolet tool.
So the 11% is less a question of CXMT's design skill than of access to equipment.

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether this is progress on the way to matching the standard, or a ceiling that stops just below its top.

The next generation settles it.
If 12,800 climbs to 14,400 within LPDDR6, multi-pass printing can reach the top after all, and if roughly the same 11% survives into the next generation, that is where the ceiling is.

Chinese memory has taken the route of entering on price and climbing toward the standard.
This number is the first time that road has been measured to the decimal.
It is also how the phrase "lithography is the last bottleneck" ends up written into a product spec sheet.

## What a long-term agreement is normally there to block

A long-term agreement is a supplier and a customer promising volumes and a price range years ahead.
Usually both sides give something up.
If prices fall the supplier does not take less than a set line, and if prices rise the customer does not pay above one.
A floor and a ceiling together.

That is where Samsung's terms stand out.

Because what is urgent on the buying side is volume, not price.
It takes more than three and a half years from breaking ground to wafers coming out, and the company expects 2027 to be tighter than this year.
For anyone building data centers, paying a few percent more is far cheaper than not getting the parts.

The contract buys a place in line rather than a price.

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether this asymmetry is something Samsung won at the table, or something today's shortage produced.

The next round of contracts settles it.
If a 5% floor on declines survives in deals signed or renewed after supply loosens, it came from bargaining power, and if a ceiling appears alongside it then, these terms were made by scarcity.

In memory, news that prices are rising has always doubled as a warning of a glut a few years out.
This time the value of the contract is set by how much less profit falls during that downturn.
The 5% cap on declines is that answer written down in advance, and whether it holds is only confirmed after prices turn.

## Why the same product lands in two different columns

Korea's trade statistics put NAND chips and SSDs in separate columns.
The chip itself counts as a semiconductor, and an SSD, which is a stack of those chips with a controller attached, counts as a computer product.

Korea has been running its largest current account surplus on record this year.
The January to May total of $141.3 billion passed the $123 billion full-year surplus of 2025, itself a record, in five months.

A current account surplus is an amount booked as earned. It is not a statement that those dollars came home.
When an exporter leaves the dollars it earned sitting in the US, the surplus grows and nothing is converted into won.

When a foreign investor sells Korean shares and leaves, the dollars going out are cash.
By the Bank of Korea's count, $110.2 billion left through equity sales between January and June.

Put simply, the ledger showed a surplus while dollars were walking out the door.

## What stopped

In the third week of July the foreign selling stopped.
This looks less like heavy buying than like fast-moving money pausing.
Once the cash stopped leaving, the surplus that had been piling up finally started to show in the rate.

## What the government did

## Why the three sit in the same kind of seat

The three dissenters have something in common.
All are presidents of regional Reserve Banks, and none is a governor on the Federal Reserve Board.

The rate-setting committee seats seven governors nominated by the president alongside five regional presidents who rotate into a vote.
This time all seven governors voted to hold.

Put simply, the people inside the house agreed, and the disagreement came from those who visit it.
It also means the new chair managed to line up the governors behind him.

## The press conference is what changed

The more important part of the day was not the vote but the press conference.
Chair Kevin Warsh's thinking fits into one line.

If the Fed does not pre-announce its decisions or hint at direction, markets will price their own read of the economy rather than the Fed's words.

That is a decision not to give forward guidance.
Forward guidance means the central bank telling you in advance what it intends to do with rates.
Ben Bernanke reached for it in 2008, when the rate could not go lower, as a way of pulling future cheap money into the present.

Since then the chair's press conference after each meeting has been where you read the next move.
Take that away and there is less reason to listen.

## What changes for markets

Remove the pre-announcement and the raw material for prices changes.
Until now the chair's words came first and the data confirmed them. Now the data comes first and the market has to interpret it alone.

The same print leaves more room for disagreement, which means bigger moves on the days data lands.
Forbes notes that Bank of America expects three quarter-point hikes this year.
With no guidance to check it against, a forecast like that gets priced as guesswork rather than confirmation.

## So what will tell us which it was

In the end the question is one.
Whether removing the pre-announcement is a normalisation that pushes markets back to the data, or a retreat that only adds volatility.

The place to look is what happens on data days.
If rate futures swing harder than they used to when inflation or jobs numbers land, the cushion guidance used to provide is gone.
If instead the stretches between meetings get quieter, markets really have started pricing the economy rather than the chair.

The 9-3 vote will matter less over time than the decision to stop talking.
The rate did not move, but the way you read the rate did.

## Why the defence industry specifically

The list makes the target obvious.
Rheinmetall is the fastest growing German defence company of Europe's rearmament period.

Dual-use goods are exactly what the name says, items used in civilian life and by the military alike.
Specialist optics, lasers, electric motors, and the rare earths that go inside them all qualify.
Put simply, what has been closed off is not weapons but the materials and parts you cannot build weapons without.

@@REF@@China hits Europe's defence industry in response to the EU's 21st sanctions package against Russia (OSW Centre for Eastern Studies, 2026-07-27)|https://www.osw.waw.pl/en/publikacje/analyses/2026-07-27/china-hits-europes-defence-industry-response-to-eus-21st-sanctions|https://www.osw.waw.pl/sites/default/files/logo_osw_300_b.png

The sanctions were meant to stop goods flowing to Russia. What came back was the supply Europe needs for its own weapons production.

## Why this kind of answer is available

A bridge is needed here.
Sanctions work where the other side depends on you, and the reverse holds just as firmly.

Europe's grounds for sanctioning those Chinese firms was that they ship goods onward to Russia.
The original piece cites studies estimating that up to 90% of sanctioned goods still reaching Russia pass through China.
That is a measure of how much of the channel Beijing holds.

But building weapons in Europe requires materials that come from the country holding that channel.
The side you can sanction and the side that can sanction you back are the same country.

## Checkers and chess

This is where the original's title metaphor lands.
Chess is a game where you work out how your opponent answers before you commit to a move.
Playing the move in front of you without counting the reply is closer to checkers.

When the sanctions list was drawn up, was anyone counting whether the other side could answer with the identical move, and what Europe would find itself short of when it did?
The reply that arrived the next day is asking whether that arithmetic was done.

## So what will tell us which it was

In the end the question is one.
Whether this counter-move is positioning for a negotiation, or a real constraint on European defence production schedules.

The place to look is delivery dates.
If Rheinmetall and other European defence firms push back delivery schedules, or announce alternative sources, it was a real constraint.
If months pass with production plans unchanged, it was closer to positioning.

A sanctions list is a list of what the other side depends on you for, and at the same time a list of what you depend on them for.
Read only one of the two and you get an answer back the next day, as happened here.

That is the first monthly decline in this index in six years.

Against a year earlier it ran 3.7%, down from 4.1% in May.
The biggest single mover was energy goods, including gasoline, which fell 9.2%.

@@REF@@Inflation rate fell by 0.1% in June, first decrease in six years (UPI, 2026-07-30)|https://www.upi.com/Top_News/US/2026/07/30/personal-consumption-expenditures-june-2026/4151785423293/|https://cdnph.upi.com/sv/ph/og/upi/4151785423293/2026/1/6002c295230d40502dff7b0b8abb84de/v1.5/Inflation-rate-fell-by-01-in-June-first-decrease-in-six-years.jpg

UPI reports that the 9.2% drop in energy goods was the largest since August 2022.
What pushed the index negative for a month, in other words, was energy rather than prices in general.

The reason markets cheered the number sits two days earlier, at the Fed meeting.
Rates were held 9 to 3, and all three dissents were for a hike rather than a cut.
Data showing prices cooling takes the wind out of the side arguing for higher rates.

## Why the Fed does not watch the CPI

Here is the part that snags.
The number we call inflation in the news is usually the consumer price index, the CPI.
But the yardstick the Fed measures its 2% target against is not the CPI. It is the personal consumption expenditures price index, the PCE.

The two are built differently.
The CPI fixes more than a hundred thousand items into a basket and prices that basket.
The PCE keeps changing what is in the basket according to what people actually bought.

When beef gets expensive, households buy more chicken.
A fixed basket cannot follow that move, so it charges the full beef increase to the index.
That failure to see shoppers switching to whatever got cheaper, which makes measured inflation run high, is called substitution bias.

## Why this statistic was a political problem

The homework in front of Congress in 1995 was the deficit.
More than half of federal spending was mandatory, programs like Social Security, and both those increases and the income tax brackets were indexed to the CPI.

Indexed means one CPI print moves spending and tax revenue at the same time.
So a finding that the CPI overstated inflation changed the arithmetic.
It would slow the growth of outlays without anyone having to vote to cut pensions.

The commission Congress set up delivered its verdict on December 4, 1996.
The CPI was overstating inflation by about 1.1 percentage points a year, and substitution bias was the largest single piece of it.

@@REF@@Final Report of the Advisory Commission to Study the Consumer Price Index (US Social Security Administration archive, 1996-12-04)|https://www.ssa.gov/history/reports/boskinrpt.html

The report itself spells out why a statistic was a money question.
If the CPI overstated the cost of living by one percentage point a year for a decade, the report calculated, the resulting addition to the deficit would reach roughly $135 billion by 2006, making it the fourth largest federal program behind Social Security, health care and defense.

The Fed's official yardstick changed from CPI to PCE in February 2000.

## Does that yardstick really read lower

@@CHK@@Headline CPI (June)|3.5%|Headline PCE (June)|3.7%|Gap|PCE higher by 0.2pp|Core CPI (June)|2.6%|Core PCE (June)|3.3%|Gap|PCE higher by 0.7pp@@The original post takes PCE to run about 0.4 percentage points below CPI. That holds as a long-run average, but June ran the other way. Energy prices fell hard, and energy carries more weight in the CPI, so the CPI came down further. Strip out food and energy and the gap widens to 0.7 points in the same direction. For this month alone, the number the Fed uses was the stricter one, not the softer one.@@Retrieved 2026-07-31 · US Bureau of Labor Statistics June CPI (released 2026-07-17) · US Bureau of Economic Analysis June PCE (released 2026-07-30)

The effect of swapping yardsticks is not the kind of thing a single month confirms.
Averages running lower and this month running lower are different claims, and this month was inverted.

## How we will know

In the end there is one question.
Is this cooling the start of a trend, or a one month energy effect.

The place it splits is oil.
What pulled June down was the drop in crude that came out of a temporary truce with Iran, and in July that truce broke and crude is rising again.
If energy turns positive again in the July print, June was a one month affair. If core prices, with food and energy stripped out, keep coming down alongside it, the trend reading holds.

The side that changed the yardstick and the side that asked for the change each had their own arithmetic.
The Fed got a target that is easier to hit, and Congress got a way to shrink the deficit without losing votes.
It is worth knowing how the number markets are cheering today was chosen.

Operating income of $2.1 million is down 90% in a year. Read on current results alone, there is nothing in this quarter to like.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · X-FAB Q2 2026 results release

## What X-FAB actually makes

A foundry builds chips on behalf of whoever designed them.
The best known ones make the phone and AI chips at the leading edge. X-FAB is not that.

This company makes analog and power semiconductors.
Chips that switch electricity on and off and change its direction, chips that turn light and sound into electrical signals.
Its main customers are automotive and industrial equipment, and those markets are weak right now.

That is where the revenue decline sits.

## So what got confirmed

@@REF@@X-FAB Q2 2026 slides: recovery signals emerge despite revenue decline (Investing.com, 2026-07-30)|https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/xfab-q2-2026-slides-recovery-signals-emerge-despite-revenue-decline-93CH-4825806

Separate from the results, the release carried three things.
Three silicon carbide design wins, several data center design wins, and a line holding volume production of photonics chips at 2028.

Silicon carbide is a material that withstands higher voltages than silicon.
As data center power distribution moves up to 800 volts, conventional silicon parts struggle and this material gets used instead.
The company naming that transition as a tailwind for its own business is what this release contained.

Photonics sits in the same place.
When the links between servers move from copper to light, someone has to build the chips that handle that light, and X-FAB puts its production at 2028.

## The income statement and the thesis are in different years

The second-quarter numbers were made by automotive and industrial equipment.
The design wins and the 2028 date are a data center story.

A design win is not revenue.
It is a customer committing to build a chip on your process, and it usually takes two to three years before that chip actually sells.
So this quarter's figures and this quarter's news point at different years.

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether the current weakness is the cost of crossing a transition, or a sign that this company's share of the new demand is small.

2027 settles it.
If those three silicon carbide design wins start showing up as 2027 revenue, the crossing is under way, and if revenue is still tied only to automotive and industrial then, the data center story lived only in the slide deck.

Third-quarter guidance is $195 million to $205 million with an EBITDA margin of 17% to 20%.
That looks above this quarter's 16.8%, so whether a recovery has started shows up first in the next set of numbers.

Situational Awareness, a hedge fund built around AI, handed over its entire listed equity book.
The buyer was Citadel.
The positions included Broadcom, Intel and CoreWeave.

@@REF@@Citadel buys most of Situational's stock holdings after AI share rout (Reuters, 2026-07-30)|https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/citadel-buys-most-situationals-stock-180422112.html|https://s.yimg.com/cv/apiv2/cv/apiv2/social/images/yahoo-finance-default-logo.png

Reuters reports that what changed hands was the part of the public portfolio financed with money borrowed from brokers.
The fund did not sell because it judged the price. The collateral behind the borrowed money ran short, and that portion went across in one piece.

Then, the next day, the same names went up.
The gains the original post recorded run from 12% to 26%.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Datacenter_Server_Racks_%2822370909788%29.jpg/960px-Datacenter_Server_Racks_%2822370909788%29.jpg|What the fund held were the companies that sell hardware and compute into AI data centers. CoreWeave rents out the GPUs slotted into racks like these by the hour.|Carl Lender · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Datacenter_Server_Racks_(22370909788).jpg

## Why only the borrowed part moved

When you post collateral with a broker and borrow to buy stock, a falling price leaves that collateral short.
The broker then asks you to top it up, and if you cannot, the broker sells for you.
That is a margin call, and the party holding the collateral is the prime broker.

Situational Awareness is reported to have run about four times leverage on its listed book.
Four times means one part your own money and three parts borrowed, buying four.
At that ratio a 25% fall in the stock produces a loss of one, which is exactly all of your own money.

In July the names the fund held fell between 35% and 47%.
That is far past 25%, so on the arithmetic the equity behind the listed book was already gone.

@@REF@@Citadel buys Situational Awareness portfolio as 4x leverage ends AI fund's 1,000% run (Tech Times, 2026-07-30)|https://www.techtimes.com/articles/322285/20260730/citadel-buys-situational-awareness-portfolio-4x-leverage-ends-ai-funds-1000-run.htm|https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/470616/citadel-buys-situational-awareness-portfolio-4x-leverage-ends-ai-funds-1000-run.jpg

The same report says former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner started the fund in late 2024 with $225 million and compounded it past 1,000% after fees.
Cut the line at the end of June this year and it was up 439%.

The size of the fund is reported differently in different places.
Reuters puts it near $20 billion under management with roughly $10 billion left after this deal, while other reports cite $45 billion at the July peak.

## What survived

One asset stayed with the fund.
Its stake in Anthropic.

Private shares are not sitting with a broker as collateral, so they cannot be margin called.
It was not kept because anyone preferred it. Whatever was pledged went first, in order.
Where leverage is involved, the person choosing what to protect is not the portfolio manager.

## Why it went up the next day

@@CMP@@Reading it as the selling ending|The forced seller that had been pressing the market all month is gone. That says the fall was about flows rather than earnings.|Reading it as the day's news|That same day, June inflation fell month over month for the first time in six years, and Microsoft surged on cloud revenue.
The split is whether you read one day as flows or as news.

@@REF@@Microsoft soars 15%, boosting tech stocks (The Motley Fool, 2026-07-30)|https://www.fool.com/coverage/stock-market-today/2026/07/30/stock-market-midday-july-30-microsoft-soars-15-boosting-tech-stocks/|https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.content.foolcdn.com%2Fimages%2F1umn9qeh%2Fproduction%2Fe3bcbb36c955ac33b4d67641805fcca8e9fca941-1401x1251.png%3Fw%3D800%26q%3D75%26fit%3Dmax%26auto%3Dformat&w=1200&op=resize

The Motley Fool reports that the Nasdaq posted its biggest single day gain since June, carried by the jump in Microsoft's Azure revenue.
Semiconductor names rode that move as well, which makes it hard to credit the whole day's gain to the liquidation finishing.

## How we will know

In the end there is one question.
Was July's decline the market repricing AI, or borrowed money leaving the building.

The place it splits is the next few weeks.
If the same names hold their ground now that the forced seller is gone, July was made by flows. If they slide again, the repricing reading was right.

Nothing was sold because conviction wavered.
The moment the price fell more than 25%, the selling side was set automatically, and the party that made that decision was the lender rather than the fund.
Where leverage is involved, collateral sets the timetable, not conviction.

Profitability at Samsung's foundry business improved sharply from a year ago, and the company said a turnaround is not far off.
Utilization at advanced nodes of 8nm and below has reached peak levels, and better yields and price increases came on top of that.

@@REF@@Samsung Electronics Announces Second Quarter 2026 Results (Samsung Newsroom, 2026-07-30)|https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-second-quarter-2026-results|https://img.global.news.samsung.com/global/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/29111731/Samsung-Corporate-More-Stories-Second-Quarter-2026-Reults_Thumb932.jpg

## So what actually lifted the revenue
The company named two reasons for higher foundry revenue.
Demand for HBM base dies grew, and volume arrived from a North American customer's products.

@@REF@@Samsung Electronics to break ground on 2nd fab in Taylor within this year (The Korea Times, 2026-07-30)|https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/business/companies/20260730/samsung-electronics-to-break-ground-on-2nd-fab-in-taylor-within-this-year|https://newsimg.koreatimes.co.kr/2026/07/30/db274b33-ff4a-4858-830e-09cf557a9bc7.jpg

A base die is the chip that sits at the bottom of an HBM stack.
It is the layer that organizes signals between the stacked DRAM above it and the GPU outside, and it is built on a foundry line, not on a memory line.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg/960px-DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg|Server DRAM. So when memory sells well, foundry revenue rises with it.
The part that improved because outside customers came back and the part that improved because Samsung's own memory sold well are mixed inside one number.

## How far along is 2nm
Based on production experience with its first generation 2nm process, the company said it will begin the full ramp of second generation 2nm in the second half.
In the second quarter it took 2nm work from one large cloud provider and from high performance computing customers, and it said talks with major customers including Broadcom are widening.
It expects the number of 2nm projects won this year to more than double from last year.

## When does output from today's construction arrive
The first Taylor fab is preparing to operate this year, and groundbreaking on the second is planned by year end with mass production targeted for 2030.
With more inquiries about 1.4nm, the company is also reviewing securing one more fab.

@@REF@@Samsung to Break Ground on Texas Fab 2 by Year-End, Target 2030 Output (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-07-30)|https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/07/30/samsung-to-break-ground-on-texas-fab-2-by-year-end-target|https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/07/30/news-p.v1.20260730.bbcf0b54510b45098aad5c199c891530_P1.jpg

That article adds that the first Taylor fab began operating this year.
So the gap from groundbreaking to output is four years, and that gap is the substance of the company's admission that advanced node expansion has not kept up with demand.

It is the same structure as memory, where the company has said wafers from a new plant take more than three and a half years to appear.
Capacity decided today does not solve today's shortage.

## Where do the older processes go
Mature nodes are shifting away from volume competition toward products that can command a higher price.
The company said it is adding capacity for 8nm and 17nm, image sensors, and the nonvolatile memory embedded inside chips.
It also named silicon capacitors and silicon photonics as areas it is growing.

## So what will settle it
The question comes down to one thing. Is the foundry recovery outside customers returning, or Samsung's own memory pulling it along.

If 2nm project wins really do more than double this year and Broadcom volume shows up as a contract, the first reading holds.
If the numbers keep improving while the customer list does not lengthen, the foundry cools together with memory once the memory boom cools.

Running memory and foundry inside one company was called a weakness for years.
This quarter that structure held the foundry up. The same structure works in the other direction too.

## What a multi-year contract actually is
An LTA locks in volumes, and often prices, for years ahead.
When prices rise, the supplier takes less than it could have. When prices fall, the customer pays more than it would have.
It works less like a sale and more like insurance both sides buy from each other.

Here are the terms Samsung described.
The base term is five years, with a further year added through negotiation each year.
The contracts carry advance payments, money handed over before any goods ship.
The company said it has already received about a quarter of the advance payments it agreed to.

Five large global data center customers have signed. Five more large customers are in final negotiations.

## Why lock it in now
The reason the company gave is time, not price.
From breaking ground on a new fab to wafers coming out takes more than three and a half years.
So even with higher capex across the industry, supply cannot expand meaningfully before 2028.
The company expects the 2027 shortage to be worse than this year's.

NAND is inside the contracts too.
NAND is the storage-side memory that keeps its contents with the power off, and server SSDs for AI machines are expected to make up more than 60 percent of Samsung's NAND revenue, up more than 20 percentage points from a year earlier.

## Who gets the remaining 30 to 40 percent
This is why the number missing from the release matters.
If 60 to 70 percent of capacity leaves through contracts, buyers outside those contracts are bidding for the other 30 to 40 percent.
The company said it set the ceiling there to keep enough flexibility for customers without agreements.
Smaller phone and PC makers, plus the spot market, compete for that slice.

## So what tells us which it was
It comes down to one question. Is locking 60 to 70 percent of capacity into five-year deals a seawall or a ceiling?

If memory prices keep climbing, it is a ceiling. Committed volume does not collect the higher price.
If prices turn down, it is a seawall. Committed volume still ships when the spot bid disappears.
Having the advance payments already in hand looks like preparation for the second case.

Memory has been an industry where everyone expands when prices rise, and that expansion returns as oversupply a few years later.
If these contracts are an attempt to break that loop, the test is how much less profit falls in the next downturn.

## What the missing 219 trillion won was

At a KOSPI of 9,100 on June 19, the fund's year-to-date paper gain stood at 314 trillion won.
With the index closing at 5,663 on July 29, the same calculation gives 95 trillion won.

A paper gain is the amount written into the books for an asset that has risen in price but has not been sold.
It is not money in hand. It is an estimate of what the money would be if sold.
So when the price retreats, the entry is erased with it.

By the original post's arithmetic, delaying the fund's depletion date by one year costs 49 trillion won.
That makes 314 trillion won worth 6.4 years and 95 trillion won worth 1.9 years.

## How we will know

In the end there is one question.
Is the buying that resumed in late July the safety net returning, or simply what falls out once the weight has drifted back under the cap.

The 116 billion won bought on July 28 and 338 billion won on July 29 are far larger than the 48 billion won of June 8 or the 29 billion won of July 7.
Set against the 573 billion won of March 13, 2020, they are still small.

If the next halt brings buying in the trillions of won, the constraint has genuinely loosened. If the figure falls back to the low hundreds of billions, this week's purchases were the mechanical result of a weight that had already come down.

Acting as the market's safety net was never the fund's objective.
The objective is return, and the safety net was a by-product of chasing it.
What remains is that this year the by-product went missing.
